rationale: A wins because it turns the same update into four real desks without making the facts wear a costume. Its "Khan Academy says its AI tutor added weeks of learning — by its own yardstick" names the tension a reporter would actually chase; B's "while rivals still charge for it" invents the market contrast before proving rivals, prices, or even that this is the competitive split. B has two usable angles, but the unsupported category play and padded teacher-workload angle make the set workshopable, not press-ready.
gaps_in_A: "AI tutoring is about to reach a million more public-school students" slightly overstates the supplied fact; the update says US school districts, not explicitly public-school students.
"30 districts signing on simultaneously" turns a rollout to 30 more districts into a simultaneous-signing pattern. That needs confirmation or softer wording.
"Khan Academy answers the independent-thinking critics directly" assumes Khan will engage the criticism. The facts only say some educators question the effect on independent thinking.
A does not isolate the teacher lesson-planning feature as its own workload angle. That may be thin, but it is a real stakeholder thread in the update.
gaps_in_B: "while rivals still charge for it" is invented. The update says Khanmigo is free and donor-funded, not that competitors charge or that the market is splitting free versus paid.
"which tends to center on students" invents a coverage-history claim. Nothing in the update supports what most Khanmigo coverage has focused on.
"teachers already stretched thin" imports a workload and burnout peg that is not in the facts, then asks for time-saved proof it does not have.

"A local-news angle on 'which 30 districts are getting Khanmigo' — duplicate" is a bad refusal. Named districts could create real local hooks; the actual problem is missing district names, not duplication.
